prompt: In the `describe` output, what does the first node in a partition's `Replicas` list name?

choices.text: The node that holds the oldest copy
choices.why: All copies hold the same log; the order says something else.

choices.text: The preferred leader
choices.why: Right. Leadership is moved back to it after a failure.

choices.text: The active controller of the cluster
choices.why: That is `LeaderId` in `kafka-metadata-quorum.sh`, not a partition's list.

choices.text: The node whose disk the topic was created on
choices.why: Every replica's node has a directory for the partition; none is the origin.

prompt: Why does the lesson give `kafka-topics.sh` two addresses, `localhost:9092,localhost:9093`?

choices.text: Each address returns half of the partitions
choices.why: Any node can answer for the whole cluster.

choices.text: To reach the cluster even when one of those nodes is down
choices.why: Right. After node 2 was killed, a WARN for 9093 and then the answer from the other address.

choices.text: Because a replication factor of 3 needs at least two bootstrap servers
choices.why: The replication factor does not constrain the client's address list.

choices.text: So that the tool writes to two leaders at once
choices.why: `describe` writes nothing; it reads metadata.

prompt: After `./cluster.sh new 3` and a topic with 3 partitions and replication factor 3, how many `sales-*` directories exist across all nodes?
How does a follower get the leader's new records?

choices.text: It fetches them from the leader, as a consumer would
choices.why: Right. Followers pull, at their own pace.

choices.text: The leader pushes each write to it and waits
choices.why: That is the common wrong picture; nothing is pushed.

choices.text: The controllers copy the segments between nodes every second
choices.why: Controllers keep metadata; data moves by fetch.

choices.text: The producer sends every record to each replica
choices.why: The producer talks only to the leader.

prompt: The leader has offsets 0 to 9, one in-sync follower has 0 to 8 and the other 0 to 6. Which offsets can a consumer read?
hint: Look for the first offset missing from some in-sync replica.

choices.text: 0 to 9, everything the leader has
choices.why: Records above the high watermark are not given to consumers.

choices.text: 0 to 8
choices.why: The slowest in-sync replica decides, and it only has up to 6.

choices.text: 0 to 6
choices.why: Right. The high watermark is 7, the first offset not on every in-sync replica.

choices.text: None until all three have offset 9
choices.why: Everything below the high watermark is readable now.

prompt: Why are consumers never shown records above the high watermark?

choices.text: Those records are still compressed
choices.why: Compression has nothing to do with visibility.

choices.text: Otherwise a reader would see records a new leader lacks, which then disappear
choices.why: Right. That rule makes a failover invisible to readers.

choices.text: Kafka reads them in batches of seven
choices.why: Seven was this example's high watermark, not a batch size.

choices.text: The producer has not received its acknowledgement yet, and acknowledgements are what make a record readable
choices.why: With acks=1 a producer can be answered before the high watermark moves; visibility follows the replicas, not the answer.

prompt: What is the default `replica.lag.time.max.ms` the broker reported?

choices.why: Right: thirty seconds without being fully caught up removes a follower.
300 is `leader.imbalance.check.interval.seconds`, in seconds.
That number was not what the grep printed.
The grep printed a larger value.

prompt: Node 3 is frozen with `kill -STOP`. Forty seconds later, what does `describe` show?

choices.text: Node 3 still in every ISR, because its process is alive
choices.why: Alive is not enough; it stopped fetching.

choices.text: Node 3 out of every ISR, and partition 2 led by another node
choices.why: Right. A frozen leader answers nobody, so leadership moved.

choices.text: Every partition offline
choices.why: Two copies stayed in sync on every partition.

choices.text: Node 3 removed from the `Replicas` list
choices.why: `Replicas` is the assignment; only `Isr` shrinks.

prompt: Why did Kafka stop counting how many messages a follower was behind, and use only time?

choices.text: Counting messages was too slow on large topics
choices.why: The cost of counting is not the reason given.

choices.text: Time is easier to configure
choices.why: Ease is not the argument; false removals are.

choices.text: Message counts differ between partitions of the same topic
choices.why: True, and irrelevant to why followers were removed wrongly.

choices.text: A burst of writes put healthy followers out of the ISR
choices.why: Right. A time limit only removes a follower that is truly stuck.

prompt: With `acks=1`, when is the producer told yes?

choices.text: When the request leaves the producer
choices.why: That is `acks=0`, where nobody answers.

choices.text: When the leader has written it to its own log
choices.why: Right. The followers may not have it yet.

choices.text: When every in-sync replica has it
choices.why: That is `acks=all`.

choices.text: When a consumer has read it
choices.why: No setting waits for a consumer.

prompt: With node 3 down and `min.insync.replicas=3`, `acks.py --acks all` reported `_MSG_TIMED_OUT`. Where was the reason `NotEnoughReplicas` found?

choices.text: In the producer's output, beside each failed sale
choices.why: The client reported its own timeout, not the broker's reason.

choices.text: In the `describe` output, in the `Elr` column
choices.why: `Elr` was empty; it is not where refusals are recorded.

choices.text: In the broker's `server.log`
choices.why: Right. grep found NotEnoughReplicasException there: an ISR of 2 against 3.

choices.text: In `__consumer_offsets`
choices.why: That topic holds consumer positions, not errors.

prompt: A topic has replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=1`. Two nodes die and producers use `acks=all`. What is true?

choices.text: Writes are refused until a node returns
choices.why: With a floor of 1, an ISR of one is enough.

choices.text: Writes are accepted on a single disk, which is acks=1 under a better name
choices.why: Right. The floor is what stops `all` from meaning just the leader.

choices.text: Writes go on with three copies, because `acks=all` always waits for every replica
choices.why: It waits for the ISR, which has shrunk to one.

choices.text: The producers switch to `acks=0`
choices.why: The client never changes its own setting.

prompt: With replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`, how many nodes can be lost while `acks=all` writes still succeed?
While the leader of partition 1 was killed, `acks.py` sent a hundred sales. What did it report?

choices.text: 70 delivered and 30 failed
choices.why: Nothing failed in the run with one node killed.

choices.text: 100 delivered, none twice
choices.why: Right. The client kept the sales in memory and sent them to the new leader.

choices.text: 100 delivered and 3 duplicates
choices.why: The offsets ran 290 to 389, exactly one per sale.

choices.text: An error, because the bootstrap address was dead
choices.why: It had three addresses and the FAIL lines are logs, not failed sales.

prompt: Node 2 comes back after being killed. What happens to the leadership it held?

choices.text: It takes it back as soon as it is in the ISR
choices.why: A returning node comes back as a follower.

choices.text: It stays with the node that took over, until a preferred election moves it back
choices.why: Right. Automatically every 300 seconds, or at once with the tool.

choices.text: It is lost, and the partition has to be recreated
choices.why: Nothing is recreated; leadership just moves.

choices.text: It moves to the active controller
choices.why: Partition leadership and the controller vote are separate roles.

prompt: What did the failure of a leader cost the producer, according to the section?

choices.text: Every sale sent while the leader was down
choices.why: None was lost: 100 of 100 delivered.

choices.text: A duplicate of each sale in flight
choices.why: The offsets show none was written twice.

choices.text: A few seconds
choices.why: Right. The partition had no leader briefly, and sales waited in memory.

choices.text: The consumer group's committed offsets
choices.why: Committed offsets live in a replicated topic and survive.

prompt: In Kafka 4, what replaced ZooKeeper for the cluster's metadata?

choices.text: A group of controllers voting with KRaft
choices.why: Right. They keep the metadata in `__cluster_metadata`.

choices.text: The schema registry
choices.why: The registry is lesson 6 and stores schemas, not cluster metadata.

choices.text: The leader of partition 0 of every topic
choices.why: Partition leaders store data; controllers decide.

choices.text: A file each broker keeps beside its log
choices.why: A file per broker could not keep them in agreement.

prompt: Nodes 2 and 3 are killed, leaving node 1. `kafka-topics.sh --create` is run against node 1. What happened?

choices.text: The topic was created on node 1 alone
choices.why: Creating a topic needs a decision, which needs a majority.

choices.text: It failed at once with connection refused
choices.why: Node 1 answered; the command waited.

choices.text: It hung until `timeout` ended it with status 124
choices.why: Right. One voter of three cannot decide anything.

choices.text: Node 1 became the only voter and created it
choices.why: The survivor does not guess that it is the survivor.

prompt: Why would a team run five controllers rather than four?

choices.text: Four controllers cannot elect a leader
choices.why: They can; they just survive no more failures than three.

choices.text: Five survive two failures; four survive one, like three
choices.why: Right. A majority of four is three, so a fourth machine buys nothing.

choices.text: Kafka requires an odd number and refuses to start with four
choices.why: It does not refuse; an even number is just wasteful.

choices.text: Five controllers process writes faster
choices.why: More voters make agreement slower, not faster.

prompt: `till-log` shows `Leader: none` and `Elr: 2`. What does the `Elr` entry tell an operator?

choices.text: Node 2 is the replica that lost the most data
choices.why: The opposite: it holds every committed record.

choices.text: Node 2 must be removed from the topic
choices.why: It is the node to bring back, not to remove.

choices.text: Node 2 is being elected leader at this moment by the controllers
choices.why: It is down; it can only be elected when it returns.

choices.text: Node 2 has all that was committed
choices.why: Right. It was the last in-sync replica, so it has everything committed.

prompt: After the unclean election made node 3 leader of `till-log`, how many sales did a consumer reading from the beginning get?
A topic holds the live positions of delivery vans, useless after a minute. Which choice about unclean election fits it, by the section's argument?

choices.text: Leave it off, because acknowledged records must never be lost
choices.why: That is the argument for sales; here an outage is worse than a gap.

choices.text: Turn it on for this topic: an hour of nothing is worse than a few lost points
choices.why: Right. It is a decision per topic, and this data is only worth anything fresh.

choices.text: Raise the replication factor to 5 instead
choices.why: That makes the situation rarer, and is a different trade at a high price.

choices.text: Turn it on for the whole cluster
choices.why: Sales and stock would then lose data silently too.

prompt: Which of these does a replication factor of 3 multiply? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The disk a topic uses
choices.why: Yes: 32,443 bytes on each of three nodes.

choices.text: Traffic between brokers
choices.why: Yes: each follower fetches every record.

choices.text: The number of partitions
choices.why: The topic still has three partitions; each has three copies.

choices.text: The number of messages a consumer reads
choices.why: A consumer reads each record once, from the leader.

prompt: Why does this lab not demonstrate what replication is really for?

choices.text: The three nodes share one machine, so no rack or zone is ever lost
choices.why: Right. Every failure here was a process ending.

choices.text: Kafka disables replication on a single machine
choices.why: Replication really happened: three identical segment files.

choices.text: `kill -9` is gentler than a real failure
choices.why: It is as abrupt as a power cut for the process.

choices.text: The followers in a lab never leave the ISR
choices.why: Node 3 left the ISR when it was frozen.

prompt: The setting that tells Kafka which failure domain a broker sits in, so replicas are spread across them, is `broker.___`.
Put the steps of the unclean election in the order they happened.
items: Ten sales written to both replicas
Ten more sales written to node 2 alone
Node 2 is killed and node 3 comes back
Node 2 returns and truncates its log

pairs.right: no decisions until a majority returned
